items.value: All three — steel slag is used in road bases, as an agricultural soil amendment and in cement manufacture
items.reasoning: Steel slag is a hard, dense, angular by-product of steelmaking, which makes it an excellent aggregate for road sub-base and base courses (1). Being rich in calcium and silicon and alkaline in reaction, it is used as a liming agent and silicate fertiliser to correct acid soils and supply micronutrients (2). Granulated slag has latent hydraulic properties and is blended into Portland slag cement, which is why steel plants supply it to cement makers (3). All three uses are established, so D.

items.value: Askot Wildlife Sanctuary and Gangotri National Park — both high-altitude Himalayan habitats
items.reasoning: The Himalayan musk deer is an animal of steep, forested and alpine slopes roughly between 2,500 and 4,500 metres. Askot Wildlife Sanctuary in Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand, was in fact created primarily for musk deer conservation (1), and Gangotri National Park in the upper Bhagirathi valley lies squarely in its altitudinal range (2). Kishanpur Wildlife Sanctuary (3) is a lowland terai forest of the Dudhwa landscape in Uttar Pradesh, and Manas (4) is a Brahmaputra floodplain and foothill park in Assam; neither reaches the altitude musk deer need.

items.value: Copper slag, cold mix asphalt technology and geotextiles are the environmentally preferred choices
items.reasoning: Copper slag (1) is an industrial waste reused as aggregate, avoiding fresh quarrying. Cold mix technology (2) uses bitumen emulsion at ambient temperature and so avoids the heating of aggregate and binder, cutting fuel use and emissions sharply — it is promoted under PMGSY for exactly this reason. Geotextiles (3) strengthen weak subgrades and reduce the thickness of aggregate needed. Hot mix asphalt (4) is the energy-intensive alternative that cold mix is meant to replace, and Portland cement (5) is one of the most carbon-intensive materials in construction. Hence 1, 2 and 3 only.

items.value: All three statements are correct
items.reasoning: Coal ash concentrates the trace elements present in coal, including arsenic, lead and mercury, which is why fly ash ponds are a heavy-metal leaching hazard (1). Burning coal oxidises its sulphur and atmospheric nitrogen, releasing sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen, the precursors of acid rain (2). Indian coal is of Gondwana origin, formed by drift deposition, and characteristically has high ash content of about 30 to 45 per cent with low sulphur (3). All three are correct.

items.value: All three — biochar serves as a growing medium in vertical farming, supports nitrogen-fixing microbes and improves water retention
items.reasoning: Biochar is a porous charcoal-like material made by pyrolysis of biomass. Its porosity and low bulk density make it a component of soilless and vertical-farming growing media (1), and that same pore structure holds water against drainage, extending the medium's water-retention time (3). Statement 2 is the judgement call: biochar's pores provide refuge and habitat for soil microbes and it raises pH and supplies micronutrients such as molybdenum and boron, and field trials report enhanced biological nitrogen fixation by rhizobia in biochar-amended media, so it is accepted as correct. Runner-up C, which takes 1 and 3 only, follows if statement 2 is treated as an over-claim.

items.value: A licence or prior permission is needed to cultivate a Schedule VI plant
items.reasoning: Schedule VI was inserted into the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 by the 1991 amendment and lists specified plants such as the blue vanda, ladies' slipper orchid, pitcher plant, red vanda, beddomes' cycad and kuth. Section 17A prohibits picking, uprooting, possessing, selling or transporting them, but Section 17B and the licensing provisions expressly allow cultivation with the prior permission of the Chief Wild Life Warden. So cultivation is regulated, not forbidden, which rules out B. C is wrong because Schedule VI has nothing to do with genetic modification, and D is wrong because the schedule protects threatened native plants, the opposite of invasive species.

items.value: Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul were ports handling foreign trade
items.reasoning: All three are coastal sites known from classical and Gupta-age trade. Ghantasala lies near the Krishna delta on the Andhra coast and appears in accounts of the eastern maritime trade; Kadura is named among the western seaboard trading harbours; and Chaul, south of present-day Mumbai in Raigad district, was a long-lived port on the Konkan coast trading with West Asia. Their common thread is location on the sea and a commercial rather than political or religious identity, which rules out capitals, art centres and pilgrimage sites.

items.value: All three are advantages of zero tillage
items.reasoning: Zero tillage sows directly into undisturbed soil through the previous crop's residue, so wheat can be drilled into standing paddy stubble without burning it — the principle behind the Happy Seeder (1). It also underlies direct seeded rice, in which paddy seed is sown straight into the field, dispensing with the nursery and transplanting of seedlings (2). Because the soil is not inverted, organic matter is not oxidised and residue is retained on the surface, so soil organic carbon builds up, giving carbon sequestration (3). Note also that statements 1 and 3 are plainly correct and no option offers those two alone, which independently confirms D.

items.value: Cassava, damaged wheat grains, rotten potatoes and sugar beet — 1, 2, 5 and 6
items.reasoning: The National Policy on Biofuels, 2018 widened the feedstock base for ethanol to include sugar-containing materials such as sugar beet and sweet sorghum (6), starch-containing materials such as corn and cassava (1), and damaged food grains such as broken rice and wheat unfit for human consumption (2) along with rotten potatoes (5). Groundnut seeds (3) and horse gram (4) are edible foodstuffs and are not in the notified list — the policy's whole design is to use surplus, damaged or non-food material rather than divert edible produce. Hence 1, 2, 5 and 6 only.

items.value: The monetary value of the long-term damage done by one tonne of carbon dioxide emitted in a given year
items.reasoning: The Social Cost of Carbon is defined as the present value, in money terms, of the total future damages caused by emitting one additional tonne of carbon dioxide in a particular year — covering losses from changed agricultural yields, health effects, property damage from flooding and so on. It is used to price the externality of emissions in policy cost-benefit analysis. B describes fossil fuel dependence, C describes climate adaptation by a displaced person, and D describes an individual carbon footprint; none of them is a damage-cost measure per tonne.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct — black gram is grown in both kharif and rabi seasons
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: black gram (urad) is a kharif crop in northern and central India and is also grown as a rabi and summer crop in the south and in rice-fallow areas, so it spans both seasons. Statement 2 is wrong: gram (chana) is the dominant Indian pulse at roughly two-fifths of production, while green gram accounts for well under a tenth — nowhere near half. Statement 3 is wrong: rabi pulse production, led by gram, has risen substantially over the past three decades rather than falling.

items.value: Cotton
items.reasoning: The description is the standard set of cotton's climatic requirements: it is a subtropical crop, hard frost kills it, it needs at least 210 frost-free days, 50 to 100 centimetres of rainfall, and a light, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil — the black cotton and alluvial soils of India. Jute is ruled out because it needs a hot humid climate with 150 to 200 centimetres of rainfall and grows on new alluvium. Sugarcane needs a longer growing period, heavier soils and 75 to 150 centimetres of rain. Tea needs 150 to 250 centimetres of well-distributed rainfall on sloping land, far above the range given.

items.value: Neither statement is correct — solar power runs submersible pumps and piston pumps as well
items.reasoning: Both statements assert a restriction that does not exist. Solar photovoltaic power drives a motor, and the motor is indifferent to where the pump sits, so solar submersible pumps for deep borewells are standard equipment under the PM-KUSUM programme, refuting statement 1. Likewise solar power runs positive-displacement pumps, including piston and diaphragm types, which are in fact preferred for low-discharge, high-head applications because they work well at the variable power a solar array delivers; that refutes statement 2. Hence neither.

items.value: Statements 1 and 4 are correct — bud chip settlings save seed material, and tissue-cultured settlings can be used
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the bud chip method scoops out only the bud with a small piece of surrounding tissue and raises it in a nursery, cutting seed cane requirement from several tonnes per hectare to a fraction of it. Statement 4 is correct: tissue-culture raised settlings are a recognised route to disease-free, genetically uniform planting material. Statements 2 and 3 are both wrong and for the same underlying reason — a sett with more buds carries larger food reserves in its internodes, so multi-budded setts give better germination and better survival under adverse weather than single-budded setts, not worse.

items.value: Crop diversification, legume intensification and tensiometer use — vertical farming is not counted
items.reasoning: Crop diversification (1) breaks monoculture, reduces pest pressure and eases the water demand of paddy-wheat rotations. Legume intensification (2) fixes atmospheric nitrogen biologically and cuts urea use. The tensiometer (3) measures soil moisture tension so that irrigation is applied only when the soil needs it, and it is promoted in Punjab precisely to save groundwater. All three are recognised eco-friendly practices in Indian agriculture. Vertical farming (4) is a controlled-environment production technology that is land- and water-efficient but heavily dependent on artificial lighting and climate control, and it is not an established eco-friendly agricultural practice in the Indian context. Runner-up D, if vertical farming is credited on its water and land savings alone.

items.value: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct; rock phosphate cannot be applied through fertigation
items.reasoning: Fertigation delivers dissolved nutrients through the irrigation water. Acids can be injected along with the fertiliser to neutralise bicarbonates and control the alkalinity of the irrigation water, which is routine practice in drip systems (1). Nutrients reach the root zone in solution and in small frequent doses, raising their availability to the plant (3) and reducing losses below the root zone through leaching (4). Statement 2 is wrong: rock phosphate is virtually insoluble in water and would clog emitters, and phosphatic fertilisers in general are difficult in fertigation because phosphate precipitates with the calcium and magnesium in irrigation water — only highly soluble forms such as phosphoric acid or mono-ammonium phosphate can be used, so the claim that 'all other phosphatic fertilizers' can be efficiently applied fails.

items.value: Chromite, kyanite and sillimanite are major minerals; bentonite has been declared a minor mineral
items.reasoning: Under the MMDR Act the Centre lists minor minerals, and everything not so listed is a major mineral. Chromite is a metallic ore and unquestionably a major mineral, which by itself eliminates options B and C. Kyanite and sillimanite are refractory raw materials reported in the Indian Bureau of Mines' major mineral statistics, so 3 and 4 also qualify. Bentonite (1) was among the minerals notified as minor minerals in 2015, alongside items such as brick earth, fuller's earth, marble and ordinary sand, and so falls outside the major category. The pivot in this item is the classification of bentonite; option A follows only if bentonite is still treated as major.

items.value: Both statements are correct
items.reasoning: Ocean Mean Temperature is the mean temperature of the water column measured down to the depth of the 26 degree Celsius isotherm, which in the south-western Indian Ocean during January to March lies at about 129 metres, so statement 1 is correct as printed. Statement 2 is correct because that is the entire purpose of the index: OMT integrates heat over the whole column rather than just the skin, so it is a more stable predictor than sea surface temperature, and Indian researchers have shown that the January to March OMT in this region correlates with whether the following monsoon's rainfall will be above or below the long-period average. The specific 129-metre figure is what makes this an item of recall rather than reasoning, hence the moderate confidence.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 are correct; fertilizer retail prices are not fully market-driven
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: the maximum retail price of urea, which is the bulk of Indian fertiliser consumption, is statutorily fixed by the Government and the gap from the cost of production is met by subsidy, so retail prices are administered rather than market-driven. Statement 2 is correct: ammonia is synthesised by the Haber-Bosch process using hydrogen derived from natural gas, which is why urea plants are gas-based and why gas prices drive the urea subsidy. Statement 3 is correct: elemental sulphur, used to make the sulphuric acid that digests rock phosphate into phosphoric acid, is recovered as a by-product of desulphurising crude oil at refineries.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; the Park does contain human habitation
items.reasoning: Desert National Park in western Rajasthan extends across the districts of Jaisalmer and Barmer, so statement 1 is correct. It is among the last strongholds of the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard, so statement 3 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the park was notified over an inhabited desert landscape and dozens of villages and hamlets with their livestock lie inside its boundaries, which is central to the management conflict there — the presence of settlements and grazing is one of the recognised pressures on bustard habitat.

items.value: Siachen Glacier lies to the north of the Nubra Valley
items.reasoning: The Siachen Glacier lies in the eastern Karakoram, and its meltwater forms the Nubra river, which flows south-east down the Nubra valley to join the Shyok. The glacier therefore sits at the head of, and to the north of, the Nubra valley. Aksai Chin lies well to the east and south-east of Siachen, so A is wrong; Leh lies to the south, so 'east of Leh' in B is wrong; and Gilgit lies far to the west, so Siachen is east of it rather than north, ruling out C.

items.value: Pairs 1 and 3 are correct — Bhilsa is in Madhya Pradesh and Girinagar in Gujarat
items.reasoning: Bhilsa is the historic name of Vidisha, near Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh, so pair 1 is correct. Girinagar is Girnar near Junagadh in Gujarat, the site of the Ashokan rock edicts and the Sudarshana lake inscriptions, so pair 3 is correct. Pair 2 is wrong: Dwarasamudra is Halebidu in Karnataka, the Hoysala capital, not in Maharashtra. Pair 4 is wrong: Sthanesvara is Thanesar in Kurukshetra district, Haryana, the seat of the Pushyabhutis and Harshavardhana's early capital, not in Uttar Pradesh.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — CGWA was set up under the Environment (Protection) Act and India has the world's largest groundwater-irrigated area
items.reasoning: Statement 2 is correct: the Central Ground Water Authority was constituted in 1997 under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, following a Supreme Court direction, which is why its regulatory notifications are issued under that Act. Statement 3 is correct: India is the world's largest user of groundwater, irrigating close to 40 million hectares from wells and tubewells, more than China and the United States combined. Statement 1 is wrong: the Central Ground Water Board's assessment is made for blocks and other assessment units rather than districts, and the over-exploited plus critical share is well below the 36 per cent figure claimed. Since 2 and 3 are both correct, B is the only option that holds them together.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct — some cyclones develop an eye, and the eye is warmer, not cooler
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: jet streams are a feature of both hemispheres, with subtropical and polar front jets in each. Statement 2 is correct: a clear eye forms only in intense, well-organised tropical cyclones; weaker tropical storms and all temperate cyclones lack one. Statement 3 is wrong and is the reverse of the truth: air subsiding in the eye is compressed and warms adiabatically, so a tropical cyclone has a warm core and the eye is several degrees warmer than its surroundings, not about ten degrees cooler.

items.value: Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve has the largest Critical Tiger Habitat
items.reasoning: Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam, spread across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana in the Nallamala hills, is India's largest tiger reserve, and its notified Critical Tiger Habitat runs to roughly 2,600 square kilometres. That is well ahead of the Sundarbans at about 1,700, Ranthambore at about 1,100 and Corbett at about 820 square kilometres. Size of the reserve as a whole is the useful cue here, and Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam is by a wide margin the largest of the four.
